title: Clinical evaluation of artificial intelligence for CT (computed tomography) head interpretation in the emergency department
official: Systematic Assessment of the Medical Utility of Radiology Artificial Intelligence (SAMURAI) for CT Head Interpretation
summary:
Background and study aims
Patients attending the Emergency Department (ED) with head injury or neurological symptoms often need a CT scan to check for serious problems such as bleeding in the brain. Specialist radiologists typically review these scans, but increasing demand can lead to delays, which may slow diagnosis and treatment decisions.

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can now analyse CT head scans immediately after they are performed and highlight scans that may contain serious abnormalities. This may help prioritise urgent cases and support clinicians in making faster and more accurate decisions.

The SAMURAI-CT study aims to find out whether using an AI tool to assist with CT head interpretation can reduce delays in reporting, improve patient flow through the Emergency Department, and maintain patient safety. It will also assess whether AI can support emergency clinicians in interpreting scans and whether its use is cost-effective for the NHS.

Who can participate?
Adult patients (aged 18 years and over) who attend the Emergency Department and undergo a non-contrast CT head scan as part of their usual care may be included.

Patients are not individually recruited, as the study uses routinely collected hospital data. Patients can opt out of their data being used via the NHS national data opt-out system or local study information provided at participating sites.

Patients under 18 years of age and those not undergoing CT head scans as part of routine ED care are not included.

What does the study involve?
The study will take place across multiple NHS hospital sites in England and will run over 12 months. During this time, the AI tool will be switched on and off at different periods (“AI On” and “AI Off”) at each site to allow fair comparison with standard care.

All patients will receive standard care regardless of whether the AI tool is in use. The AI system is a decision support tool only and does not replace clinicians, who remain responsible for all diagnosis and treatment decisions.
Researchers will securely collect and analyse data from routine hospital systems, including electronic patient records and radiology systems. 

These data will be used to assess:
•	Time taken to produce radiology reports
•	Time to clinical decisions (such as discharge or admission)
•	Length of stay in the Emergency Department
•	Detection of clinically important findings
•	Patient recalls and safety events

A subgroup of trained emergency clinicians will also have their scan interpretations assessed to evaluate how accurately CT head scans are interpreted when supported by AI.

Patients will not be required to attend additional visits or undergo extra tests as part of this study.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
The AI tool may help clinicians prioritise urgent cases and reach decisions more quickly, which could reduce waiting times in the Emergency Department and improve patient experience.

The risks to patients are minimal. The AI tool is used only as a support system, and clinicians will always make the final care decisions. There is a small risk that findings could be missed or incorrectly highlighted, but this will be closely monitored throughout the study. All patients receive standard care, with no additional procedures.

Where is the study run from?
The study is led by Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust and delivered across multiple participating NHS hospital sites.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The study includes an initial setup and testing phase, followed by a 12-month trial period, with additional time for data analysis and reporting (approximately 24 months in total).

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) through its Invention for Innovation (i4i) programme, within the Transformative and Disruptive Innovations scheme.

Who is the main contact?
SAMURAI.CT@ouh.nhs.uk
conditions: Non-contrast CT head scans requested through emergency department
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
All patients undergoing non-contrast CT Head Scans in the emergency department will be eligible for inclusion
Exclusion criteria:
1. They are aged under 18 years (for patient and public groups)
2. They lack the capacity to give informed consent 
3. They are unable to complete study procedures in English (for survey and DCE components) 
4. Patient has opted out of data sharing on the National Data Opt-Out 
5. Patient completes the opt out questionnaire displayed on posters in the waiting room
